Newly hatched Clouded salamander larvae emerge from their gelatinous egg masses at a snout-vent length of approximately 1 centimeter [Lb = approximately 1 centimeter], a modest size typical of hynobiid amphibians. Embryonic development proceeds within the aquatic egg, and at a constant water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the time from egg deposition to eclosion lasts roughly 24.5 days [ab = roughly 24.5 days]. This relatively brief incubation period reflects the species' adaptation to cool, montane streams where early spring snowmelt provides critical breeding habitat. The endotrophic larvae, still reliant on yolk reserves, begin exogenous feeding shortly after hatching, transitioning to a diet of small aquatic invertebrates. The yolk-sac resorption marks the onset of active feeding, and the free-swimming tadpoles enter a phase of rapid somatic growth that will continue until the approach of metamorphosis.

The larval period culminates in metamorphosis, a process of substantial morphological transformation including gill resorption, limb bud development, and skin keratinisation. At the completion of this larval-juvenile transition, the newly metamorphosed individuals exhibit a snout-vent length of 1.8 centimeters . This size at metamorphosis represents a near doubling of the birth length, achieved over a growing season that depends on local thermal conditions and food availability. Post-metamorphic juveniles then disperse into the surrounding terrestrial habitat, where they assume a fossorial lifestyle beneath logs and leaf litter. The terrestrial juvenile phase is a period of continued growth and foraging, during which the young salamanders must build up adequate body condition to support eventual gonadal maturation.

Sexual maturation in male Clouded salamanders occurs upon reaching a snout-vent length of approximately 5.5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 5.5 centimeters], though some field records indicate that puberty may also be achieved at a slightly smaller size of 5 centimeters [Lp = 5 centimeters]. This intraspecific variation in size at maturity likely reflects differences in local resource availability and thermal regimes across the species' fragmented range. Under laboratory conditions maintained at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the time elapsed since birth at which males attain puberty is approximately 5 years since birth [tp = approximately 5 years since birth]. This protracted pre-reproductive period is consistent with a relatively slow life-history strategy, a common pattern among temperate-zone salamanders that inhabit resource-limited environments.

Adults ultimately reach a maximum snout-vent length of 7.8 centimeters [Li = 7.8 centimeters], which represents the asymptotic body size for the species. Corresponding to this ultimate length, the maximum recorded adult wet weight is approximately 5 grams [Wwi = approximately 5 grams], a modest mass that places Hynobius nebulosus among the smaller members of its genus. Reaching this adult size requires several years of post-metamorphic growth, and the species' relatively high longevity reflects this extended developmental trajectory. At a constant environmental temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the maximum documented lifespan from birth to natural death is around 24.2 years [am = around 24.2 years]. This remarkable longevity is among the highest recorded for any hynobiid salamander, a feature likely linked to the species' low metabolic demands and the predictable, cool conditions of its montane forest habitat.

Females deposit their eggs in gelatinous, paired egg sacs attached to submerged rocks or vegetation in slow-moving streams. Each female typically produces a single clutch per breeding season, with fecundity estimates based on field collections indicating approximately 30 to 50 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 30 to 50 eggs per clutch]. The breeding frequency is constrained to one reproductive event per year [F_R_i = one reproductive event per year], a pattern that aligns with the species' slow life-history pace and the short duration of suitable spawning conditions in early spring. This annual reproductive schedule, combined with the extended juvenile period and high adult survivorship, suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes stability and longevity over high fecundity. Such a demographic profile renders the species particularly vulnerable to habitat disturbance and climate change, which could disrupt the thermal and hydrologic cues essential for successful reproduction.
